title: Halves: two equal parts

summary.text: You cut a dosa into two pieces. Is each piece a half? Only if the two pieces are equal. You will cut paper dosas, share beans between two plates, pour water and fold cloth. You will find out how to make two equal parts, and how to check them. You will find that some groups cannot be shared into two equal groups, because one thing is left over. You will also find that no real dosa is ever cut into two perfectly equal parts, so people agree on what is equal enough.
summary.art: A girl at a kitchen table laying one half of a folded paper circle on top of the other half, with two small plates of beans beside her.

intro.hook: Kavya and Arun share 8 laddus like this. Did each child get half?
intro.text: No. Kavya has 5 laddus and Arun has 3. Half means one of two equal parts. Half of 8 laddus is 4, so a fair share is 4 for Kavya and 4 for Arun. Two parts are not always two halves. In this unit you will cut paper dosas and share beans. You will find out when two parts are halves, and when they are not.
intro.art: Two steel plates side by side, one with five laddus and one with three, and two children looking at them.

outcomes: I can tell whether two parts are equal or unequal, and check by putting one part on top of the other.
I can cut or fold one whole thing into two halves, and say that two halves make the whole again.
I can find half of a group of up to 20 things by sharing them into two equal groups.
I can say which groups can be shared into two equal groups, and which leave one over.
I can make quarters by halving a half, and say that four quarters make the whole.
I can say that real things are never cut into perfectly equal parts, so people agree on what is equal enough.

terms.meaning: All of one thing, or all of one group, with nothing missing.
terms.example: One dosa before you tear it is a whole dosa. All 8 laddus in the box are the whole group.
terms.art: One round dosa on a plate, uncut, with a loop drawn around all of it.

terms.meaning: A piece of a whole thing, or some of a whole group.
terms.example: You tear a dosa in two. Each piece is a part of the dosa.
terms.art: A dosa torn into two pieces, with an arrow pointing to each piece.

terms.meaning: The same amount. Not more and not less.
terms.example: 4 laddus on your plate and 4 laddus on my plate are equal.
terms.art: Two plates with four laddus each, and an equals sign between them.

terms.meaning: Not the same amount. One is more and one is less.
terms.example: 5 laddus on one plate and 3 on the other are unequal.
terms.art: Two plates, one with five laddus and one with three.

terms.meaning: One of two equal parts of a whole. Two halves make the whole.
terms.example: You fold a dosa down the middle and tear along the fold. Each piece is half of the dosa.
terms.art: A dosa folded down the middle, then shown as two matching pieces.

terms.meaning: To give everyone the same amount.
terms.example: You have 6 murukkus. You give one to your sister, one to yourself, and go on. Each of you gets 3.
terms.art: Two children with a plate each, a hand putting one murukku on each plate in turn.

terms.meaning: What remains when a group cannot be shared equally.
terms.example: You share 7 beans between two plates. Each plate gets 3, and 1 bean is left over.
terms.art: Two plates with three beans each and one bean alone between them.

terms.meaning: One of four equal parts of a whole. You get quarters when you halve each half.
terms.example: You fold a towel in half, and then in half again. Open it. The folds show 4 quarters.
terms.art: A towel opened flat with two fold lines crossing, making four equal parts.

explanations.context: In the Half Test you cut paper dosas into two pieces. Some pieces matched and some did not. This card gives the words for that.
explanations.definition: Two parts are equal when they are the same amount. They are unequal when one is more than the other.
explanations.description: Here is how to check. Put one part on top of the other. If no edge sticks out, the parts are equal. If one part sticks out, that part is bigger, and the parts are unequal. Here is a worked example. Amma tears a dosa in two. You lay your piece on your brother's piece. Your piece sticks out all around. So your piece is bigger, and the two parts are unequal. For things you count, such as laddus, you check by counting. 4 and 4 are equal. 5 and 3 are unequal. Now look at the picture. Which pair of pieces is equal?
examples: A banana broken near one end gives a long part and a short part. They are unequal.
A sheet of paper folded edge to edge and cut on the fold gives two equal parts.
6 beans on one plate and 6 on the other are equal. 7 and 5 are unequal.
explanations.art: Two paper circles, each cut in two: one cut down the middle with the pieces stacked and matching, one cut near the edge with the big piece sticking out under the small one.

explanations.context: This card says exactly what the word half means. You made halves in the Half Test when you folded a paper dosa and cut along the fold.
explanations.definition: When one whole is cut into two equal parts, each part is called a half. Two halves put together make the whole again.
explanations.description: A half needs two things. There must be two parts, and the parts must be equal. Two unequal parts are just a big part and a small part. Neither one is a half. Here is a worked example. Take a square of paper. Fold it so that one edge lies exactly on the edge across from it. Press the fold. Cut along the fold. Lay one piece on the other. They match, so each piece is half of the square. Put them side by side and you have the whole square again. There is more than one way to make halves. You can fold the square from side to side, from top to bottom, or from corner to corner. Each way gives two halves.
examples: Half a dosa and the other half make one whole dosa.
Half a glass of buttermilk fills the glass up to the middle.
People say 'the bigger half' when they talk. In maths there is no bigger half. If one part is bigger, the parts are not halves.
explanations.art: A round dosa with a fold line down the middle, one side shaded, and the words 'one half' on each side.

explanations.context: This card shows how to find half of a group of things, such as 8 murukkus. You did this with beans and two plates in the Half Test.
explanations.definition: Half of a group is one of two equal groups that make up the whole group.
explanations.description: You cannot fold a group of murukkus. So you share them out. Here is a worked example. There are 8 murukkus and two plates. Put one murukku on the first plate and one on the second. Do it again, and again, until none are left. Now count one plate. It has 4. Count the other. It also has 4. So half of 8 is 4. You can check by adding the two halves. 4 and 4 make 8, the whole group. Now you try. Use 6 beans and two plates. What is half of 6?
examples: Half of 10 groundnuts is 5 groundnuts.
Half of 2 idlis is 1 idli.
A box has 12 crayons. Half of them, 6 crayons, are on the table. The other half are still in the box.
explanations.art: Eight murukkus being dealt one at a time onto two steel plates, ending with four on each.

explanations.context: In the Half Test, 7 beans would not share into two equal groups. This card says why, and what you can do about it.
explanations.definition: Some groups can be shared into two equal groups. Others always leave one thing over.
explanations.description: Share 7 beans between two plates. Each plate gets 3, and 1 bean is left. If you give that bean to one plate, the plates are 4 and 3. That is unequal. So 7 beans cannot be put into two equal groups of whole beans. The same thing happens with 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. These are called odd numbers. With 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 nothing is left over. These are called even numbers. What can you do with the one left over? It depends on the thing. You can cut a banana in half, so 7 bananas can be shared as 3 and a half each. You cannot cut a marble or a kitten in half. Then one stays over, or someone gets one more.
examples: 9 groundnuts: 4 on each plate and 1 left over.
10 groundnuts: 5 on each plate and none left over.
3 dosas for two people: one whole dosa each, and the last dosa cut into two halves. Each person gets one and a half.
explanations.art: Two plates with three beans each and a seventh bean alone in the middle, with a question mark over it.

explanations.concept: A real half is never perfectly equal
explanations.context: In the Half Test, even your best folded halves did not match perfectly. This card asks what that means for the word half.
explanations.description: Look very closely at your two best paper halves. One edge wobbles a little. One piece is a hair wider. Now think of a real dosa. One half has more crisp edge. One half has more potato. Nobody can cut a real thing into two perfectly equal parts. With numbers it is different. Half of 8 beans is 4 beans, exactly. But are the 4 beans on each plate the same? No two beans are the same size. So people agree on what is equal enough. For dosas, it is enough when nobody wants to swap. An old rule helps: one person cuts, and the other person chooses first. Then the one who cuts tries hard to make the parts equal. People do not all agree on what this tells us about halves.
examples: A shop sells half a kilo of rice. The scale stops at half a kilo, but it cannot count every grain.
A carrom board has two halves. A carpenter measured them, as closely as the ruler shows.
Half of 10 is 5. That is exact, because it is about numbers and not about things.

perspectives.who: The view that a half is an agreement
perspectives.explanation: In the real world there are no perfect halves. A half is two parts that are equal enough for the people sharing. People decide how close is close enough.

perspectives.who: Plato, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,400 years ago, and many mathematicians since
perspectives.explanation: The exact half is real. It is an idea, and you can think it perfectly clearly. The dosa pieces are rough copies of it. You can only say 'these are not quite equal' because you already know what equal means.

explanations.art: Two paper half-circles laid one on the other, seen very close up, with a thin sliver of the lower one showing along the edge.

explanations.context: This card is about the words people use for a half in English, Tamil and Hindi.
explanations.definition: Half means one of two equal parts. Many languages have a special word for it.
explanations.description: The word half does not sound like the word two. The same is true in some other languages. In Tamil, two is irandu and half is arai. In Hindi, two is do and half is aadha. People needed a word for half so often that they gave it a word of its own. Listen at the vegetable shop. In Tamil Nadu you may hear 'arai kilo', which is half a kilo. Tamil has a word for a quarter too, which is kaal. Half of a quarter is araikkaal. That word is made of arai and kaal, half and quarter.
examples: English: half a dosa. Tamil: arai dosai. Hindi: aadha dosa.
A half-litre packet of milk holds half as much as a one-litre packet.
Half past six on a clock means half of an hour has gone by since six.
explanations.art: A vegetable seller's scale with a small heap of tomatoes, and the words half, arai and aadha written above it.

explanations.concept: Halves in the day, the sky and the Earth
explanations.context: This card shows where halves turn up far from the kitchen: in the Moon, in day and night, and on the Earth.
explanations.definition: A half is one of two equal parts. The sky and the Earth show parts that are very nearly halves.
explanations.description: Look at the Moon about a week after the new Moon. You see a shape like half a circle. Half of the side facing us is lit by the Sun. At any moment, about half of the Earth is in sunlight and about half is in the dark. That is why it is day in India when it is night on the other side of the world. Twice a year, near 20 March and near 22 September, day and night are almost the same length everywhere. That day is called an equinox. Day and night are still not exactly equal on that day. The daytime is a few minutes longer. So these halves are like the dosa halves. They are close, but not perfect.
examples: A half Moon looks like the letter D or like a D turned around.
When it is noon in Chennai, it is around midnight on the other side of the Earth.
On an equinox, day and night are each about 12 hours long.
explanations.art: The Earth seen from space with one side lit and one side dark, and a small half-lit Moon beside it.

rows.label: the Earth right now: lit and dark
the Moon you see, a week after new Moon

explanations.concept: Other living beings make halves too
explanations.context: This card is about a groundnut seed, a tiny bacterium and your own first day of life. Each one shows halving in a living being.
explanations.description: Humans are not the only living beings who halve. Take a groundnut and rub off the thin red skin. Press gently. The seed opens into two halves that match. A bean and a chana do the same. Many plants build each seed as two matching halves, with the tiny baby plant between them. Now think of a bacterium, a living being too small to see. One kind is called E. coli, and they are shaped like a tiny rod. To make a new bacterium, one of them grows longer and then splits across the middle into two. In 2008, scientists measured where the split falls. It was very close to the exact middle, but usually a tiny bit off. You did this too. You began as one single cell. After about a day, that cell split into two cells. About a day later there were four. What people argue about is whether to call this maths.
examples: A groundnut seed opens into two halves that fit together like two cupped hands.
Toor dal is a seed called pigeon pea, with the skin taken off and the two halves split apart.
One E. coli bacterium becomes two bacteria of nearly the same length.

perspectives.who: The view that this is maths
perspectives.explanation: The bacterium finds their own middle and the plant builds two matching halves. Finding a middle and making two equal parts is what halving is. They do it without words or numbers.

The bacterium uses chemicals that move from end to end inside the cell and leave the middle free. That is a way of finding the middle, but nobody knows of any counting or measuring behind it. They say it is safer to call it halving, and to leave the word maths open.

explanations.art: A groundnut seed opened into two matching halves with the tiny baby plant at one end, next to a rod-shaped bacterium pinching in at the middle.

explanations.concept: Stretch: half of a half is a quarter
explanations.context: This card goes further than Class 1. It is for a child who finds halves easy.
explanations.definition: When a whole is cut into four equal parts, each part is called a quarter. Four quarters make the whole.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Fold a strip of paper in half and open it. You see 2 halves. Fold it in half again, and then once more the same way. Open it. Now you see 4 equal parts. Each part is a quarter of the strip. Each half was cut into two, so 2 quarters make one half. This works for groups too. Half of 8 beans is 4 beans. Half of those 4 beans is 2 beans. So a quarter of 8 beans is 2 beans. A quarter is smaller than a half of the same thing, because the whole was shared among more parts.
examples: A towel folded in half and in half again has 4 layers. Each layer is a quarter of the towel.
A dosa cut in half, with each half cut in half, gives 4 quarters.
Half of 12 is 6. Half of 6 is 3. So a quarter of 12 is 3.
explanations.art: A paper strip shown three times: whole, folded into two halves, and folded into four quarters, with one quarter shaded.

agreed.text: Two pieces are halves only when the two pieces are equal.
agreed.evidence: You can test it. Cut a paper circle near the edge. Lay the small piece on the big piece. The big piece sticks out, so neither piece is a half.

agreed.text: Two halves put together make the whole again.
agreed.evidence: Put your two paper halves side by side. You get the whole circle back. Add the two halves of 8 beans, 4 and 4, and you get 8 again.

agreed.text: Some groups of things cannot be shared into two equal groups of whole things.
agreed.evidence: Share 7 beans between two plates, one at a time. However you do it, one bean is left over. The same happens with 1, 3, 5 and 9 beans.

agreed.text: A bacterium called E. coli splits into two parts that are very nearly equal in length.
agreed.evidence: In 2008, scientists used a computer to measure photographs of these bacteria as they split. The split was very close to the middle of the cell (Guberman and others, 2008).

challenging.claim: If you cut something into two pieces, each piece is a half.
challenging.who: Many young children, and many grown-ups when they talk fast
challenging.context: This card is about a common mix-up between two pieces and two halves.
challenging.for: A half is always one of two parts. In daily talk, people often say 'half' for any one of two pieces.
challenging.against: In maths, the two parts must also be equal. A big piece and a small piece are two parts, but neither one is a half.

challenging.claim: A perfect half is real, even if nobody can cut one.
challenging.context: This card is about an old argument: is an exact half real, or only something people agree on?
challenging.for: Everyone means the same thing by an exact half. Half of 8 is 4 for everybody, everywhere. That is hard to explain if a half is only an agreement.
challenging.against: Nobody has ever seen or made an exact half of a real thing. Every real cut is a little off. What people really use is 'equal enough'.

challenging.context: This card is about whether halving belongs only to people.
challenging.for: Only humans are known to talk about halves, check them and argue about them.
challenging.against: A bacterium splits very close to their own middle. A groundnut plant builds each seed as two matching halves. Whether to call that maths is argued about, but the halving is real.

big_questions.q: You cut a dosa into two pieces. How can you find out if they are halves?
big_questions.hint: What happens when you lay one piece on top of the other?

big_questions.q: Why can 8 beans be shared into two equal groups, but 7 beans cannot?
big_questions.hint: Share them one by one. What happens to the last bean?

big_questions.q: How many different ways can you fold a square of paper into two halves?
big_questions.hint: Side to side. Top to bottom. Corner to corner. Are there more?

big_questions.q: Is anything in the world exactly equal to anything else?
big_questions.hint: Look at two leaves from one tree, or your own two hands.

big_questions.q: Can everything be shared in half? What about a song, a puppy or a hug?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a cycle if you cut it in half? What happens to a banana?

big_questions.q: Two people share a dosa. Who should decide if the two parts are fair?
big_questions.hint: The one who cuts? The one who chooses? Both?

story.title: The Sweeter Half
story.note: Selvi, Muthu, Paati and Appa are made up. It is true that many families in Tamil Nadu buy sugarcane for Pongal. It is true that the joints of a sugarcane are closer together near the bottom, and that the bottom part is usually sweeter than the top.
text: On the morning of Pongal, Paati came home from the market with one stick of sugarcane. The cane was taller than Appa. The stalk was purple and shiny, with a tuft of green leaves at the top.
"One cane," said Paati. "Half for Selvi and half for Muthu. Not a finger more for either of you."
Selvi was seven. Her brother Muthu was nine, and he liked to be in charge.
"I will find the middle," said Muthu. "It is easy."

He laid the cane on the veranda floor. A sugarcane has rings around it, like the rings on a finger. Muthu counted the parts between the rings. "Ten parts. Half of ten is five." He counted five parts up from the bottom and tapped the ring there. "Cut here, Appa."
Selvi looked at the cane. Then she lay down on the floor next to it, with her feet at the bottom end. The ring Muthu had tapped was only as high as her knee.
"That is not the middle," she said. "The parts at the bottom are short. The parts at the top are long. You counted five small ones for me and five big ones for you."
Muthu looked again. She was right. The five parts at the bottom were squeezed close together. The five parts at the top were each as long as his hand.
"Counting the parts only works if the parts are equal," said Selvi.
"Fine," said Muthu. "Then I will measure with my hand." He walked his hand along the cane from end to end. "Nine hands, and a little bit." He frowned. "What is half of nine and a little bit?"
Nobody could say exactly. Not even Appa.

Selvi went into the house. She came back with the ball of banana string that Paati used for tying flowers. She held one end of the string at the bottom of the cane. She rolled the ball along to the top, and Appa snipped the string there.
Now the string was exactly as long as the cane.
Selvi picked up the two ends of the string and held them together in one hand. The string hung down in a loop. She ran her other hand down to the bottom of the loop and pinched it.
"This is the middle of the string," she said. "Both sides are the same, so it has to be."
She laid the string along the cane again, with her fingers still pinching the fold. "So this is the middle of the cane."
It was far above the ring that Muthu had tapped. Appa marked the spot with his thumbnail.
"Wait," said Paati from the doorway. She was smiling. "Before you cut. Which half do you want, Selvi? The bottom or the top?"
"They are the same," said Selvi. "I measured."
"The same length," said Paati. "But the bottom of a cane is sweeter than the top. Everybody who has grown sugarcane knows that."
Selvi and Muthu looked at each other. Then they both said, "I want the bottom!"
They argued until the pongal pot on the stove began to hiss. Muthu said he was older. Selvi said she had found the middle. Appa waited with the big knife and said nothing.

Selvi sat down next to the cane and looked for a long time. She looked at the string in her hand. She had folded the string end to end. But a cane had another middle too. It ran the long way, from the bottom all the way up to the leaves.
"Appa," she said. "Do not cut it across. Cut it the long way. Down the middle, from top to bottom."
Appa laughed. He stood the cane up and set the knife on the top end. He tapped it with a block of wood, and the cane split slowly, all the way down, with a sound like a door creaking.
Now there were two long halves. Each one had a sweet bottom and a plain top.
Muthu held the two halves side by side. One was a little thicker near the leaves. He looked at Selvi, and he did not say anything about it.
"You chose the cut," he said. "So I choose the half." And he took the one that was nearest to him.
story.epiphany: For the parent: two parts are halves only if they are equal, and 'equal' depends on what you are sharing. Muthu's first cut gave two parts, but the parts were unequal in length. Selvi's fold found the middle, because folding lays one part exactly on the other. Then Paati showed that equal length was not equal sweetness. Cutting the long way gave halves that were equal in both.
ask: Muthu counted five parts for each child. Why was that not a fair share?
How did folding the string help Selvi find the middle of the cane?
The two short pieces would have been the same length. Why would they still not be a fair share?
What is something at home that you could cut in half in two different ways?

experiments.title: The Half Test: two parts, but are they halves?
experiments.context: In this test you cut three paper dosas into two pieces each, and you share beans between two plates. Each time, you guess first whether the two parts will be equal. You will find out what makes two parts halves.
experiments.question: When one thing or one group is made into two parts, are the two parts always halves?
experiments.predict: Before each cut and each sharing, guess: will the two parts be equal or unequal? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The three paper dosas are the same size, because we draw them around the same plate. We check every pair of pieces the same way, by laying one on the other. We share the beans the same way every time, one for each plate in turn.
results_table: What we made into two parts

materials.item: old newspaper or used paper, to make 3 paper dosas
a steel plate to draw around, about as wide as your hand is long
scissors
a pencil, and a sheet of paper for the table
dried beans such as rajma or chana, or buttons
two small plates or katoris

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts with sharp scissors, or sits beside the child while they cut. Keep beans, seeds and other small things away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Cut three paper dosas in three ways and check the pieces. Then share 8, 6, 10, 12, 7 and 9 beans between two plates.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws the table. For each cut and each sharing, write the guess and what you found. At the end, the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the table.

flow.do: 1. Draw around the plate three times and cut out three paper dosas. 2. Take dosa A. Cut it in two with one straight cut far from the middle. 3. Hold up the two pieces. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Your child lays one piece on the other. 5. Write the guess and what you found.
flow.say: I cut this dosa into two pieces. Is each piece a half? Why do you think so? How could we check?
flow.kid: Here are two pieces of one paper dosa. Are they equal? Guess. Then lay one on the other.

ask.q: What do you see when one piece lies on the other?

flow.parent: Cut off about a third, so the difference is easy to see. Many six-year-olds say 'yes, half', because there are two pieces. Do not correct it. Let the pieces answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Half Test, where you cut paper dosas and share beans to see which parts are halves. A paper dosa is cut far from the middle.

flow.do: 1. Give your child dosa B and the scissors. 2. Ask them to cut it into two equal parts, without folding. 3. Ask for a guess: will the pieces match? 4. Your child lays one piece on the other. 5. Write the guess and what you found.
flow.say: Now you cut. Try to make two equal parts, just by looking. Do you think they will match? Why?
flow.kid: Cut dosa B into two equal parts. Do not fold it. Then check if they match.

ask.q: How close did you get? Where does one piece stick out?
good: This side is a bit bigger.

flow.parent: A cut by eye is usually close but not equal. That is the finding. Praise the careful checking, not the cut.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Half Test, where you cut paper dosas and share beans to see which parts are halves. You cut a paper dosa by eye and check the pieces.

flow.do: 1. Hold up dosa C. 2. Ask how you could make the two parts match, and wait for ideas. 3. If no idea comes, fold the dosa so that the edges meet all the way round. 4. Press the fold. Cut along it. 5. Your child checks the pieces, then puts them side by side to make the circle again.
flow.say: What could we do to this dosa before cutting, so that the two parts match?
flow.kid: Fold dosa C so the edges meet. Press the fold. Cut on the fold. Check the pieces.

ask.q: Why does folding first help?
good: The two sides lie on each other.
The fold is in the middle.
You can see they match before you cut.

ask.q: Put the two pieces side by side. What do you get?

flow.parent: Each of these two pieces is a half. Say the word now, for the first time: 'When the two parts are equal, each one is called a half.'
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Half Test, where you cut paper dosas and share beans to see which parts are halves. You fold a paper dosa before cutting it.

flow.do: 1. Put 8 beans in a heap and the two plates beside it. 2. Ask for a guess: can the plates get equal shares, and how many each? 3. Your child shares the beans, one for each plate in turn. 4. Count each plate. 5. Do the same with 6, 10 and 12 beans. Write each result.
flow.say: Here are 8 beans and two plates. Can both plates get the same number? How many do you think each will get? Why?
flow.kid: Share 8 beans between two plates. One here, one there. Count each plate. Try 6, 10 and 12.

ask.q: Each plate has 4. What is half of 8?

flow.parent: Half of 8 is 4, half of 6 is 3, half of 10 is 5 and half of 12 is 6. If your child counts out a heap for each plate, show sharing one by one. It always works.
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Half Test, where you cut paper dosas and share beans to see which parts are halves. You share 8 beans, then 6, 10 and 12, between two plates.

flow.do: 1. Put out 7 beans. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Your child shares them. One bean is left over. 4. Ask what could be done with it. 5. Try 9 beans. Write the results.
flow.say: Now 7 beans. Will both plates get the same number? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Share 7 beans between two plates. What happens at the end? Try 9 beans too.

ask.q: What can we do with the bean that is left over?
good: Give it to one plate, but then it is not equal.

flow.parent: 7 gives 3 and 3 with 1 left over. 9 gives 4 and 4 with 1 left over. All the ideas for the last bean are good. A bean is hard to cut. A banana would be easy.

check.q: You share 9 beans between two plates, one by one. What happens?
check.why: 4 and 4 make 8, so 1 bean is left over. Picking 5 each would need 10 beans. 9 cannot be shared into two equal groups of whole beans.

flow.context: This is step 5 of the Half Test, where you cut paper dosas and share beans to see which parts are halves. You try to share 7 beans, then 9, between two plates.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why. 3. Write their words under the table.
flow.say: Look at everything we tried. When were the two parts halves? When were they not?
flow.kid: Look at your table. When were the two parts halves? When were they not?

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why is it so?
good: Two parts are halves only when they are equal.
Dosa A had a big piece and a small piece.
7 beans left one over, so no halves.

check.q: A dosa is cut into a big piece and a small piece. Is the big piece a half?
options: Yes, it is the bigger half
check.why: No. Halves are two equal parts. Picking 'yes' usually means counting the pieces and not checking their size. In maths there is no bigger half.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Half Test, where you cut paper dosas and share beans to see which parts are halves. You say what you found.

activities.title: Half a Tumbler: halves you cannot fold or count
activities.context: In this activity you pour one full tumbler of water into two tumblers, so that each gets half. The point is to find a way to check halves when you cannot fold the thing or count it.
activities.problem: Water cannot be folded, and it cannot be counted like beans. How will you know the two parts are equal?

materials.item: steel tumblers or glasses, all the same size and shape
water
a tray or a kitchen cloth, for spills

schedule.what: Pour one tumbler of water into two tumblers in halves. Check, and pour back.

activities.record: Draw the two tumblers side by side. Draw a line on each to show where the water came up to.

setup.art: Three identical steel tumblers on a tray, one full of water and two empty.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one tumbler. Put two empty ones beside it.

setup.art: A child pouring water from one tumbler into two others, a little at a time.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the water into the two empty tumblers.

setup.art: Two tumblers side by side at a child's eye level, with the water at the same height in both.
setup.caption: 3. Stand them side by side. Is the water at the same height?

flow.do: 1. Fill one tumbler with water. 2. Put two empty tumblers of the same kind beside it on the tray. 3. Ask how the water could be shared so that each tumbler gets half. 4. Let your child pour.
flow.say: This water is for two people. Give each tumbler half. How will you know when they are equal?
flow.kid: Pour the water into the two empty tumblers. Give each one half.
flow.parent: Use tumblers of the same size and shape. With different shapes, the same height does not mean the same amount.
flow.context: This is the first step of Half a Tumbler, where you pour one tumbler of water into two equal parts.

flow.do: 1. Stand the two tumblers side by side on a flat place. 2. Your child bends down and looks from the side. 3. If one is higher, pour a little across and look again.
flow.say: Bend down and look from the side. Which one has more? What will you do about it?
flow.kid: Stand the two tumblers side by side. Look from the side. Make the water the same height.

ask.q: How do you know the two parts are equal now?
good: The water is at the same height.
They look the same from the side.

flow.parent: Standing the tumblers side by side does the job that laying one paper piece on the other did.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Half a Tumbler, where you pour one tumbler of water into two equal parts. You check the two parts by looking at the height of the water.

flow.do: 1. Ask what will happen if both halves are poured back into the first tumbler. 2. Your child pours them back. 3. Look at how full the tumbler is.
flow.say: If we pour both halves back, how full will the first tumbler be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how full the first tumbler will be. Pour both halves back in. Look.

ask.q: What did the two halves make?
good: Nearly full, a few drops spilled.

check.q: You pour two halves of a tumbler of water back into one tumbler. How full is it?
check.why: Full. Two halves make the whole. Picking 'half full' means counting only one of the halves.

flow.context: This is the last step of Half a Tumbler, where you pour one tumbler of water into two equal parts. You pour the two halves back together.

activities.title: Maths in the kitchen: Share the Snack
activities.context: In this activity you share a real snack with one other person: a banana, a dosa or roti, and a handful of groundnuts. The point is to use halves the way families use them every day, and to learn the rule 'one cuts, the other chooses'.
activities.problem: Three foods, two people. Each food has to be halved in a different way.

materials.item: a banana
a dosa, roti or slice of bread
groundnuts, grapes or pieces of murukku
plates

activities.safety: Wash hands first. No knife is needed: break the banana with the peel on, and tear the dosa along a fold.

schedule.what: At snack time, share a banana, a dosa and a handful of groundnuts into halves for two people.

activities.record: Draw the three foods, each as two halves. Under the groundnuts, write how many each person got.

setup.art: A child holding an unpeeled banana against a second banana-length strip of paper folded in half to find the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Find the middle of the banana. Break it there.

setup.art: A dosa folded in half on a plate, a child's hands tearing along the fold.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the dosa edge to edge. Tear on the fold.

setup.art: Groundnuts being put one at a time onto two plates.
setup.caption: 3. Share the groundnuts: one for you, one for me.

setup.art: Two plates each holding half a banana, half a dosa and some groundnuts, with a second child pointing at one plate.
setup.caption: 4. One person made the halves. The other chooses first.

flow.do: 1. Put the banana, the dosa and the groundnuts on the table with two plates. 2. Tell your child the rule: you make the halves, and I choose my plate first. 3. Ask why that rule might be a good one.
flow.say: This snack is for the two of us. You make the halves. Then I choose my plate first. Why is that a fair rule?
flow.kid: You will share this snack with one person. You make the halves. They choose first.

ask.q: If I choose first, what kind of halves will you try to make?
good: The same, or you will take the big one.

flow.context: This is the first step of Share the Snack, where you share real food into halves for two people. You learn the rule: one cuts, the other chooses.

flow.do: 1. Ask how to find the middle of the banana. 2. Let your child try. One way is to lay a strip of paper along it, fold the strip in half and mark the fold. 3. Your child breaks the banana at the mark, with the peel on. 4. Compare the two parts side by side.
flow.say: A banana is curved, so you cannot fold it. How could you find the middle?
flow.kid: Find the middle of the banana. Break it there. Put the parts side by side.

ask.q: Are the two parts equal? How did you check?
good: I put them side by side.

flow.parent: The two parts will not be perfectly equal. One end of a banana is thinner. Ask whether they are equal enough.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Share the Snack, where you share real food into halves for two people. You halve a banana.

flow.do: 1. Your child folds the dosa edge to edge and tears along the fold. 2. Lay one part on the other to check. 3. Put one part on each plate.
flow.say: Now the dosa. What did we do with the paper dosa to get two equal parts?
flow.kid: Fold the dosa edge to edge. Tear on the fold. Lay one part on the other.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Share the Snack, where you share real food into halves for two people. You halve a dosa by folding it.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess: will the groundnuts share equally? 2. Your child shares them, one for each plate in turn. 3. Count each plate. 4. If one is left over, ask what to do with it.
flow.say: Now the groundnuts. Do you think they will share equally, or will one be left over? Why?
flow.kid: Share the groundnuts. One for this plate, one for that plate. Count each plate.

ask.q: One groundnut is left over. What shall we do?
good: Split it. A groundnut opens into two halves.

flow.parent: A groundnut splits neatly into two halves, so the last one can be shared too.
flow.context: This is step 4 of Share the Snack, where you share real food into halves for two people. You find half of a handful of groundnuts.

flow.do: 1. Look at both plates. 2. You choose your plate first, as the rule says. 3. Ask whether your child would be happy with either plate. 4. Eat the snack.
flow.say: I choose this plate. Are you happy with the other one? Would you have been happy with either?
flow.kid: Let the other person choose a plate. Are you happy with yours? Now eat.

ask.q: When are two shares fair?
good: When I would be happy with either one.

check.q: Two people share a dosa. One cuts it. Who should choose a piece first?
check.why: The other person. Then the one who cuts tries to make the two parts equal, because they will get the piece that is left.

flow.context: This is the last step of Share the Snack, where you share real food into halves for two people. The other person chooses a plate first.

activities.title: Maths in stitching: the Tailor's Fold
activities.context: In this activity you fold paper in half, draw half of a kurta along the fold and cut it out. Tailors do the same with cloth. The point is to see that a fold gives two halves that match exactly.
activities.problem: A tailor wants the left side and the right side of a kurta to match. Drawing both sides by hand never matches. What does the tailor do?

materials.item: old newspaper or used paper
a pencil or crayon
scissors

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts with sharp scissors, or sits beside the child while they cut.

schedule.what: Draw a whole kurta by hand and check it. Then cut one from folded paper and check that.

activities.record: Keep the paper kurta. Draw a line along its fold and write 'half' on each side.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded in half, with half of a simple kurta shape drawn against the folded edge.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the paper in half. Draw half a kurta, starting at the fold.

setup.art: Scissors cutting along the drawn line through both layers of the folded paper.
setup.caption: 2. Cut along the line, through both layers. Do not cut the fold.

setup.art: The paper opened out into a whole kurta shape with a fold line down the middle and two matching sides.
setup.caption: 3. Open it. The two sides match.

flow.do: 1. On a flat sheet, your child draws a whole kurta or shirt shape by hand. 2. Cut it out. 3. Fold it down the middle and look at the two sides.
flow.say: Draw a kurta and we will cut it out. Do you think the left side and the right side will match? Why?
flow.kid: Draw a whole kurta. Cut it out. Fold it down the middle. Do the sides match?

ask.q: Fold it down the middle. Do the two sides match?

chart.title: Drawn by hand: do the sides match?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Tailor's Fold, where you cut a shape from folded paper. First you draw a whole kurta by hand and check it.

flow.do: 1. Fold a new sheet in half and press the fold. 2. Your child draws half a kurta, with the middle of the kurta on the fold. 3. Cut along the line through both layers. Do not cut along the fold. 4. Ask what the shape will look like when it is opened. 5. Open it.
flow.say: This time we draw only half, on folded paper. What will we see when we open it?
flow.kid: Fold the paper. Draw half a kurta at the fold. Cut. Guess what you will see. Open it.
flow.parent: The neck of the kurta sits on the fold, and the sleeve points away from it. If the shape falls into two pieces, the fold was cut. Try again.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Tailor's Fold, where you cut a shape from folded paper. You draw half a kurta on folded paper and cut it out.

flow.do: 1. Fold the new kurta along its fold line again and look at the edges. 2. Ask why the two sides match this time. 3. Tell your child that tailors call this 'cutting on the fold'.
flow.say: Why do the two sides match this time?
flow.kid: Fold your kurta again. Do the sides match? Why do they match this time?

ask.q: Why do the two sides match now?
good: One side was lying on the other.

check.q: You cut a shape from paper folded in half. You open it. What do you see?
options: A big side and a small side
check.why: Two halves that match. Both layers were cut with one cut, so one side is a copy of the other.

flow.parent: Tailors really do this. Many pattern pieces are placed on a fold of the cloth, so that the left and the right come out the same.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Tailor's Fold, where you cut a shape from folded paper. You check the two sides of the kurta.

activities.title: Stretch: Fold the Washing, half and half again
activities.context: In this activity you fold a towel in half, and then in half again, while helping with the washing. This goes a little past Class 1. The point is to see that halving a half gives four equal parts, called quarters.
activities.problem: A towel folded in half shows 2 parts. How many parts will it show if you fold it in half again?

materials.item: a small towel, a napkin or a handkerchief
more dry washing to fold, if there is some
a strip of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Fold a towel in half and in half again. Count the parts. Then fold the rest of the washing.

activities.record: Fold a strip of paper in half and in half again. Open it, draw a line on each fold and write 'quarter' in each part.

setup.art: A child holding a small towel by two corners and bringing them to the other two corners.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the towel in half. Make the corners meet.

setup.art: The folded towel being folded in half a second time.
setup.caption: 2. Fold it in half again.

setup.art: The towel opened flat, showing two fold lines that cross and four equal parts.
setup.caption: 3. Open it. Count the equal parts.

flow.do: 1. Your child folds the towel in half, corner to corner. 2. Ask how they know it is half. 3. Open it and count the parts the fold shows.
flow.say: Fold the towel in half. How do you know each part is a half?
flow.kid: Fold the towel in half. Make the corners meet. Open it. How many parts?

ask.q: How do you know each part is a half?
good: One part lies on the other.

flow.context: This is the first step of Fold the Washing, where you fold cloth in half and in half again.

flow.do: 1. Your child folds the towel in half, and then in half once more. 2. Before it is opened, ask for a guess: how many parts will the folds show? 3. Open the towel and count the parts.
flow.say: I fold it in half, and in half again. How many parts will we see when we open it? Why?
flow.kid: Fold in half. Fold in half again. Guess how many parts. Open it and count.

ask.q: How many parts? Are they equal?
good: Yes, they were all lying on each other.

flow.parent: Many children guess 3, one more part for one more fold. There are 4, because each of the 2 halves was halved. Each part is called a quarter.

check.q: You fold a towel in half, and in half again. How many equal parts when you open it?
check.why: 4. Each of the 2 halves is folded into 2. Picking 3 means adding one part for each fold, but the second fold cuts both halves.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Fold the Washing, where you fold cloth in half and in half again. You fold the towel in half a second time.

flow.do: 1. Fold the rest of the washing together. 2. For each piece, your child says 'half' or 'quarter' as they fold. 3. Ask which is bigger: a half of the towel or a quarter of the same towel.
flow.say: Let us fold the rest. Say half or quarter as you fold. Which is bigger, half of this towel or a quarter of it?
flow.kid: Fold the washing. Say 'half' or 'quarter' each time you fold.

ask.q: Which is bigger: half of the towel, or a quarter of the same towel?
good: Half, because a quarter is half of the half.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fold the Washing, where you fold cloth in half and in half again. You fold the rest of the washing into halves and quarters.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: Open a Seed
activities.context: In this activity you open groundnuts and look at the two halves inside each seed. The point is to see that a plant builds each seed as two matching halves.
activities.problem: What is inside a groundnut seed? Is it one piece, or more?

materials.item: groundnuts, roasted or raw, with the thin red skin on
a small plate
toor dal or chana dal from the kitchen

activities.safety: Do not do this activity if anyone at home is allergic to groundnuts. Use soaked rajma or chana seeds. Keep beans, seeds and other small things away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Open six groundnuts. Compare the two halves of each. Look at dal.

activities.record: Draw one groundnut seed opened into two halves. Show where you found the tiny baby plant.

setup.art: A child's fingers rubbing the thin red skin off a groundnut seed over a plate.
setup.caption: 1. Rub the thin red skin off a groundnut.

setup.art: A groundnut seed being gently pressed open into two halves.
setup.caption: 2. Press gently. The seed opens into two parts.

setup.art: Two groundnut halves lying flat side by side, with a tiny pointed bump at the end of one.
setup.caption: 3. Fit the parts together. Do they match? Find the tiny baby plant.

flow.do: 1. Give your child one groundnut. 2. Ask for a guess: how many parts are inside the seed? 3. Your child rubs off the red skin and presses gently until the seed opens.
flow.say: How many parts do you think are inside this one seed? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how many parts are inside the seed. Rub off the skin. Press gently.
flow.context: This is the first step of Open a Seed, where you look inside a groundnut.

flow.do: 1. Your child fits the two parts back together, then lays them flat side by side. 2. Ask whether the parts are equal. 3. Look for the tiny pointed bump at one end. This is the baby plant. 4. Open five more groundnuts and check each one.
flow.say: Fit the two parts together. Are they equal? Open more seeds. Is it the same every time?
flow.kid: Fit the two parts together. Are they equal? Open five more seeds and check.

ask.q: Are the two parts equal? What else did you find?
good: A tiny bump on one of them.

flow.parent: Every groundnut seed has two parts that match closely. The baby plant usually stays on one of them, so the two are not perfectly equal.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Open a Seed, where you look inside a groundnut. You compare the two parts of each seed.

flow.do: 1. Put a few grains of toor dal or chana dal on the plate. 2. Ask what each grain of dal might be. 3. Fit two grains together, flat sides touching.
flow.say: Look at this dal. Each grain has one flat side and one round side. What do you think a grain of dal is?
flow.kid: Look at a grain of dal. One side is flat. What do you think a grain of dal is?

ask.q: What is one grain of dal?
good: A seed that was split in two.

check.q: You rub the skin off a groundnut seed and press. How many matching parts does the seed open into?
check.why: 2. The seed opens into two parts of nearly the same size and shape. A grain of dal is one such part from another kind of seed.

flow.parent: Toor dal is the seed of the pigeon pea plant, with the skin taken off and the two halves split apart. Chana dal is a split chickpea.
flow.context: This is the last step of Open a Seed, where you look inside a groundnut. You look at grains of dal.

games.title: Half Bingo
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a bingo game with ten number cards. A card is turned over, and you cover half of that number on your grid. It builds quick halving of the numbers 2 to 20.

printables.title: Ten number cards to cut out
A bingo grid of 3 rows of 3 boxes, one for each player. Write a number in each box.

rules: Each player draws a grid of 3 rows of 3 boxes. Write nine different numbers from 1 to 10 in the boxes, in any order. One number is left out.
Mix the ten number cards and put them face down in a pile.
Turn over the top card. Everyone says half of that number.
If anyone is not sure, count out that many beans and share them between two plates.
If the half is on your grid, cover it with a bean.
The first player to cover three boxes in a row calls 'Half!' and wins. A row can go across, down or from corner to corner.
Playing alone: guess how many cards you will need before your first row. Then play and count.

setup.art: A hand-drawn grid of three rows of three boxes with the numbers 1 to 10, one missing, written in mixed order, and a pile of small cards face down.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your grid. Write nine numbers from 1 to 10.

setup.art: A card showing 14 turned face up, and a child putting a bean on the 7 on her grid.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card. Cover half of that number.

setup.art: A grid with three beans in a row going from corner to corner, and a child with her hand up.
setup.caption: 3. Three in a row wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the ten cards, or write the numbers on slips of paper. 2. Each player draws a grid and writes nine different numbers from 1 to 10 in it. 3. Give each player about 9 beans. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Write any nine numbers from 1 to 10 in your boxes. One number will be left out.
flow.kid: Draw 3 rows of 3 boxes. Write nine numbers from 1 to 10 in them.

chart.title: One way to fill a grid

flow.context: This is the first step of Half Bingo, a card game where you cover half of each number that is called. Here you make your grid.

flow.do: 1. Turn over one card as a practice. 2. Ask everyone for half of that number. 3. Check with beans: count out that many and share them between two plates. 4. Cover the half on each grid.
flow.say: The card says 12. What is half of 12? Let us check with beans.
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Say half of that number. Check with beans on two plates.

check.q: The card says 12. Which number do you cover on your grid?
check.why: 6. Share 12 beans between two plates and each plate gets 6. Picking 12 covers the whole number, not half of it.

flow.parent: For the first few games, check every card with beans. Soon your child will remember some halves without the beans.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Half Bingo, a card game where you cover half of each number that is called. Here you practise one turn.

flow.do: 1. Play the game, one card at a time. 2. Now and then, ask how a player knows the half. 3. Stop when someone has three in a row.
flow.say: The card says 16. What is half of 16? How do you know?
flow.kid: Play the game. Turn a card. Cover the half. Three in a row wins.

ask.q: How do you know half of 16 is 8?

flow.context: This is step 3 of Half Bingo, a card game where you cover half of each number that is called. Here you play until someone has three in a row.

flow.do: 1. Turn over the cards that are left, one by one. 2. Say each number and its half together.
flow.say: Let us say the ones that are left. Half of 18 is 9. Half of 20 is 10.
flow.kid: Turn over the cards that are left. Say each number and its half.
flow.context: This is the last step of Half Bingo, a card game where you cover half of each number that is called. Here you say the halves that were not called.

games.title: Roll and Share
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice game played with a bowl of beans. You roll, take that many beans and share them between your two plates. It builds quick halving, and it shows which numbers leave one over.

printables.title: A sheet with three columns, one row for each turn

rules: Put a bowl of about 50 beans in the middle. This is the bank. Each player has two plates and a cup.
On your turn, roll two dice. Count all the dots. Take that many beans from the bank.
Share your beans between your two plates, one for each plate in turn.
If the plates are equal, put the beans from one plate in your cup. That is your half. The other half goes back to the bank.
If one bean is left over, only that one bean goes in your cup. All the others go back to the bank.
The first player with 12 beans in their cup wins.
If you like, write each turn on the score sheet: what you rolled, what each plate got and what was left over.
Playing alone: count how many rolls you need to get 12 beans. Play again and try to need fewer.

setup.art: A bowl of beans in the middle of a table, with two small plates and a cup in front of each of two players, and two dice.
setup.caption: 1. Bank in the middle. Two plates and a cup for each player.

setup.art: Two dice showing 3 and 5, and a child sharing eight beans between two plates.
setup.caption: 2. Roll. Take that many beans. Share them between your plates.

setup.art: A child tipping the four beans from one plate into her cup and pushing the other plate back toward the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Equal plates: keep one half. One left over: keep only that bean.

flow.do: 1. Put the bowl of beans in the middle. 2. Give each player two plates and a cup. 3. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: We roll, take that many beans and share them between our two plates. If the plates are equal, we keep one half.
flow.kid: Put the bean bowl in the middle. Take two plates and a cup.
flow.context: This is the first step of Roll and Share, a dice game where you share beans into two equal groups. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn each. 2. Roll, count the dots, take the beans and share them. 3. Say aloud what happened: 'Half of 8 is 4', or '7 leaves one over'.
flow.say: I rolled 8. I share them. Each plate gets 4, so I keep 4. Now you try.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Take that many beans. Share them between your two plates.

check.q: You roll 3 and 4, so you take 7 beans. How many go in your cup?
check.why: 1. Seven beans share as 3 and 3 with 1 left over. When one is left over, only that bean goes in your cup.

flow.parent: For a shorter or easier game, roll one dice. Then the numbers go up to 6.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Roll and Share, a dice game where you share beans into two equal groups. Here you practise one turn.

flow.do: 1. Play until someone has 12 beans in their cup. 2. Before some rolls are shared, ask for a guess: equal plates, or one left over?
flow.say: You rolled 9. Before you share them, what do you think? Equal plates, or one left over?
flow.kid: Play the game. Guess before you share: equal, or one left over? First to 12 wins.

ask.q: Which rolls gave you the most beans? Which gave only one?
good: The big ones that share equally.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Roll and Share, a dice game where you share beans into two equal groups. Here you play until someone has 12 beans.

flow.do: 1. When the game ends, each player counts the beans in their cup. 2. Ask which rolls left one over.
flow.say: Which numbers left one bean over? Which numbers shared equally?
flow.kid: Count the beans in your cup. Which rolls left one bean over?
flow.context: This is the last step of Roll and Share, a dice game where you share beans into two equal groups. Here you count up and look back at the rolls.

projects.title: My Book of Halves: five days, five kinds of half
projects.context: In this five-day project you halve a different kind of thing each day and draw it on a page. On the last day you look for something that cannot be halved. The point is to see that halves are made and checked in different ways.
projects.problem: Paper is halved by folding. Beans are halved by sharing. What about water, a day or a toy car?

materials.item: sheets of paper, folded and stapled or tied into a small book
a pencil and crayons
things from home to halve: a leaf or paper, a fruit, grapes or beans, water

projects.safety: A grown-up does any cutting with a knife. Keep beans, seeds and other small things away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Something you fold: a sheet of paper or a fallen leaf. Draw it with the fold line.
Something you cut or break: a fruit, a roti or a biscuit. Draw the two halves.
A group: grapes, beans or crayons. Draw the two equal groups and write the numbers.
Something you pour: water or buttermilk in two tumblers. Draw the two levels.

challenges.title: Stretch: halve the dough and prove it
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. You halve a ball of chapati dough, which cannot be folded flat or counted. Then you invent a way to prove that the two parts are equal.
challenges.problem: Here is one ball of dough for two chapatis. Make two equal parts. Then prove to someone else that they are equal. 'They look the same' is not proof.
constraints: You must use all of the dough. No bits left on the table.
You must show someone else that the two parts are equal, in a way they can check.
You may use anything in the kitchen that a grown-up says is fine.
materials: a ball of chapati dough or play clay, about as big as a lemon
a clothes hanger, two paper cups or small bags of the same kind, and string
two tumblers of the same size and shape
a ruler or a strip of paper
general: Pull the ball into two pieces by eye and roll each into a ball. Put the two balls side by side.
Roll the dough into one long, even rope. Fold the rope in half and cut at the fold.
Press each part flat into the same katori, one after the other, and see how high each one comes.
creative: Make a balance. Hang one cup from each end of a clothes hanger and hang the hanger from a door handle. Put one part in each cup. If the hanger stays level, the parts weigh the same.
Let the other person choose first. If they cannot tell which part they want, the parts are equal enough.
Roll both parts into ropes of the same thickness. Lay them side by side and compare the lengths.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to prove it. Try it on your two parts. If the parts turn out unequal, move a pinch of dough across and test again.

flow.kid: Make two equal parts from the dough. How sure are you that they are equal?

ask.q: How do you know they are equal?
good: This one may be a bit bigger.

flow.parent: Most children halve by eye and say the parts look the same. That is the starting point. The challenge is to do better than looking.
flow.context: This is the first step of the dough challenge, where you halve a ball of dough and prove that the halves are equal. Here you halve the dough in your own way.

flow.do: 1. Say that looking is not proof. 2. Ask for ideas to prove it. 3. Read the usual ways and the creative ways aloud, if your child wants ideas.
flow.say: They look the same to you. How could you prove it to someone who does not believe you?
flow.kid: Looking is not proof. Think of a way to prove the two parts are equal.

ask.q: What could a clothes hanger and two cups do?
good: If it stays level they are the same.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds and uses their way of proving. 2. For the balance, tie one cup to each end of the hanger. Use string of the same length for both. Hang the hanger on a door handle. 3. Check that the empty balance hangs level. 4. Put one part in each cup. 5. If one side goes down, move a pinch of dough across and test again.
flow.say: Test your two parts. If they are not equal, what will you do?
flow.kid: Test your two parts your own way. Not equal? Move a pinch across. Test again.
flow.parent: The balance must hang level when it is empty. If it does not, slide one string along the hanger until it does.

check.q: Two dough balls sit in a hanger balance. The left side goes down. What does it mean?
check.why: The left ball is heavier, so the parts are unequal. Move a pinch of dough from left to right and test again.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the dough challenge, where you halve a ball of dough and prove that the halves are equal. Here you test your two parts and fix them.

flow.do: 1. Your child shows their proof to someone else at home. 2. Ask whether the parts are perfectly equal now, or equal enough. 3. Make two chapatis from the two parts, if it is real dough.
flow.say: Show your proof to someone. Are the two parts perfectly equal now, or equal enough?
flow.kid: Show someone your proof. Are the parts perfectly equal, or equal enough?

ask.q: Could a better balance still find a tiny difference?
good: They are never exactly the same.

items.p: One roti was torn into these two pieces. Are the pieces equal or unequal?
items.why: Equal. The two pieces are the same length, so neither one sticks out. Each piece is half of the roti.

items.p: A ribbon was cut into these two pieces. Is piece 1 half of the ribbon?
items.why: No. Piece 1 is much longer than piece 2. Halves are two equal parts, so neither piece is a half.

items.p: Count the laddus. Half of them is ____ laddus.
items.why: There are 6 laddus. Share them between two plates and each plate gets 3. So half of 6 is 3.

items.p: Two halves of a dosa, put together, make one whole dosa.
items.why: True. A half is one of two equal parts of a whole. Put both parts back and the whole is there again.

items.p: Two plates have 4 beans each. They are the two halves of a group. How many beans are in the whole group?
items.why: 8. The two halves together make the whole group. 4 and 4 make 8. Picking 4 counts only one of the halves.

items.p: Half of 10 groundnuts is ____ groundnuts.
items.why: Share 10 groundnuts between two plates, one by one. Each plate gets 5. 5 and 5 make 10.

items.p: Two plates of beans. Sort each pair: equal or unequal?
items.why: Two groups are equal when they have the same number. 3 and 3, 6 and 6, and 1 and 1 are equal. In the other pairs, one plate has more.

items.p: How much of this dosa is shaded?
items.why: Half of the dosa. The dosa is cut into two equal parts, and one of them is shaded.

items.p: Match each group to half of it.
items.why: Half of a group is one of two equal groups. 2 and 2 make 4. 4 and 4 make 8. 1 and 1 make 2. 3 and 3 make 6.

items.p: Draw a roti. Draw one line that cuts it into two halves.
items.a: A circle with one straight line through the middle, so the two sides match.
items.why: A strong drawing has the line going through the middle of the circle. If the line is near the edge, the two parts are unequal.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. In the Half Test, why were the two pieces of dosa A not halves?
items.a: Because the two pieces were unequal. One piece was bigger than the other.
items.why: A strong answer says the pieces did not match when one was laid on the other. Halves must be two equal parts.

items.p: A dosa is torn into a big piece and a small piece.

views.says: There are two pieces. So each one is a half.
They are not halves. My piece is smaller.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with the sister, because halves must be equal. The girl is right that a half is one of two parts.
items.why: Halves need two things: two parts, and the parts equal. The girl checked only the first.

items.p: Both hidden numbers are the same. Together they make 12. Each hidden number is ____.
items.why: 6 and 6 make 12. Two equal numbers that make 12 are the two halves of 12.

items.p: Count the dots. Half of them is ____ dots.
items.why: There are 14 dots. Shared between two plates, each plate gets 7. 7 and 7 make 14.

items.p: You share 5 murukkus between two plates, one by one. What happens?
items.why: 2 and 2 make 4, so 1 murukku is left over. 3 on each plate would need 6 murukkus.

items.p: 11 beans can be shared into two equal groups with none left over.
items.why: False. 5 and 5 make 10, so 1 bean is left over. 11 is an odd number.

items.p: Share each number of beans between two plates. Sort: none left over, or one left over?
items.why: 4, 10 and 12 share as 2 and 2, 5 and 5, and 6 and 6. With 7, 3 and 9, one bean has no partner on the other plate.

items.p: Meena has 7 grapes and Ravi has 5. How many must Meena give Ravi to make them equal?
items.why: 1. Then Meena has 6 and Ravi has 6. Picking 2 gives Meena 5 and Ravi 7, which is unequal the other way.

items.p: Half of a number is 9. The whole number is ____.
items.why: The two halves are 9 and 9. Together they make 18.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest amount to the biggest.
items.why: Half of 2 is 1. Half of 6 is 3. Half of 8 is 4. Half of 10 is 5. A bigger group has a bigger half.

items.p: 3 dosas are shared equally by two people. How much does each person get?
items.why: Each person takes 1 whole dosa. The last dosa is cut into two halves, one for each. So each gets 1 and a half.

items.p: Half of 20 is 10.
items.why: True. 10 and 10 make 20, so each half of 20 is 10.

items.p: Draw 10 grapes. Draw a loop around half of them.
items.a: Ten grapes with a loop around exactly 5.
items.why: Half of 10 is 5. A strong drawing has 5 grapes inside the loop and 5 outside.

items.p: 7 bananas for two children. Say how you would share them fairly.
items.a: Each child gets 3 bananas. The last banana is cut in half, so each gets 3 and a half.
items.why: A strong answer shares 6 bananas as 3 and 3, and then does something fair with the last one, such as cutting it in half.

items.p: Two friends share 9 marbles, one by one. One marble is left over.

views.says: I shared them out, so the last one is mine.
Then it is not equal. Let us keep the last one aside.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For example: 5 and 4 are unequal, so keeping one aside is the only way to stay equal.
items.why: 9 cannot be shared into two equal groups of whole marbles. The friends have to agree on what is fair. The numbers do not settle it.

items.p: This strip has 4 equal parts. Half of the strip is ____ parts.
items.why: Half of 4 parts is 2 parts. If you shade 2 of the 4 parts, the shaded and unshaded sides match.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. The strip has 4 equal parts. How much of the strip is shaded?
items.why: A quarter. A quarter is one of four equal parts. A half would be 2 of these parts.

items.p: Half of 8 is 4. Half of 4 is 2. So a quarter of 8 is ____.
items.why: A quarter is half of a half. Half of 8 is 4, and half of 4 is 2. Check: 2 and 2 and 2 and 2 make 8.

items.p: A quarter of a dosa is bigger than half of the same dosa.
items.why: False. A quarter is half of a half, so it is smaller. Four people sharing a dosa each get less than two people sharing it.

items.p: You fold a paper strip in half 3 times. How many equal parts when you open it?
items.why: 8. One fold gives 2 parts. The second fold halves each, giving 4. The third halves each again, giving 8.

items.p: Which of these is still useful after it is cut in half?
items.why: A banana. Half a banana is still food. Half a cycle cannot be ridden, and half a spoon cannot hold soup.

items.p: A real dosa can be cut into two perfectly equal parts.
items.why: False. Every real cut is a little off, and one side always has a bit more. The two parts can be equal enough that nobody minds.

items.p: Put these three in order, smallest amount first.
items.why: A quarter of 12 is 3. Half of 12 is 6. All 12 is 12.

items.p: Match each number to half of it.
items.why: Check by adding each half to itself. 10 and 10 make 20. 8 and 8 make 16. 9 and 9 make 18. 7 and 7 make 14.

items.p: Half of the children in a room are girls. There are 6 girls. How many children are in the room?
items.why: 12. The girls are one half, so the other half is also 6. 6 and 6 make 12. Picking 3 halves the 6 again.

items.p: Fold a square of paper into two halves in two different ways. Say what you did.
items.a: For example: I folded it side to side. Then I folded another one corner to corner.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different folds where the two parts lie exactly on each other. Side to side, top to bottom and corner to corner all work.

items.p: Draw a shape whose left half matches its right half. Draw the line down the middle.
items.a: A shape such as a kite, a heart, a leaf or a butterfly, with a line down the middle and the two sides matching.
items.why: A strong drawing would match if it were folded on the line. This is how the paper kurta was made.

items.p: Two thinkers argue about halves.

views.says: A perfect half is real, even if nobody can cut one.
There are no perfect halves. People just agree on equal enough.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other thinker has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason from the unit. For example: half of 8 is exactly 4, or my best paper halves still did not match perfectly.
items.why: This is a real argument with no agreed answer. Mathematicians and philosophers have held both views for more than two thousand years.

quiz.p: A ribbon is cut into two pieces like this. Are the pieces equal or unequal?
quiz.why: Unequal. Piece 1 is longer than piece 2. So these pieces are not halves.

quiz.p: How can you check that two paper pieces are equal?
quiz.why: Lay one on the other. If no edge sticks out, they are equal. Counting the pieces only tells you there are two.

quiz.p: A dosa is cut into two unequal pieces. Each piece is a half.
quiz.why: False. Halves are two equal parts. Two unequal pieces are a big piece and a small piece.

quiz.p: You have one half of a dosa. How many more halves make the whole dosa?
quiz.why: 1 more. Two halves make a whole, and you already have one of them.

quiz.p: Share these beans between two plates. Each plate gets ____ beans.
quiz.why: There are 12 beans. Shared one by one, each plate gets 6. 6 and 6 make 12.

quiz.p: Each child got 8 grapes, and that was half each. How many grapes were there in all?
quiz.why: 16. The two halves are 8 and 8, and together they make 16. Picking 4 halves the 8 again.

quiz.p: Which number of beans leaves one over when you share them between two plates?
quiz.why: 9. It shares as 4 and 4 with 1 left over. 6 shares as 3 and 3, and 10 as 5 and 5.

quiz.p: 10 beans can be shared into two equal groups with none left over.
quiz.why: True. 5 on one plate and 5 on the other uses all 10 beans.

quiz.p: This strip has 4 equal parts. What is one part called?
quiz.why: A quarter. A quarter is one of four equal parts. A half is one of two equal parts.

quiz.p: A napkin is folded in half, and in half again. Opened, it shows ____ equal parts.
quiz.why: 4. The first fold makes 2 halves. The second fold halves each of them, so there are 4 quarters.

quiz.p: Why do we call two dosa halves 'equal enough'?
quiz.why: No real cut is perfect. One side always has a little more. People agree that the parts are close enough to call halves.

quiz.p: Two people want to share a banana fairly. One breaks it. What should the other do?
quiz.why: Choose first. Then the one who breaks it tries to make the two parts equal, because they get the part that is left.

applications: A shopkeeper sells half a kilo of rice or half a litre of milk. In Tamil Nadu you may hear 'arai kilo'.
A tailor folds cloth in half and cuts both layers together, so the left and right sides of a kurta match.
A cook halves a recipe when only half as many people are eating.
A kabaddi match is played in two halves. In the Pro Kabaddi League each half is 20 minutes, and the teams change sides in between.
A carpenter finds the middle of a plank before fixing a handle or a hinge there.
A doctor may tell a grown-up to give a child half a tablet. The grown-up breaks it along the line in the middle.
A clock says 'half past six' when half an hour has gone by since six.
Two families who share the cost of an auto ride each pay half.

open_questions.q: Is a perfect half real, or only an idea in our heads?
open_questions.why_open: Mathematicians and philosophers have argued about this for more than two thousand years. No test has settled it.

open_questions.q: Is anything in the world exactly equal to anything else?
open_questions.why_open: Every time people measure more closely, they find small differences. Nobody knows whether two real things can ever be exactly equal in every way.

open_questions.q: How does a bacterium find their own middle so well?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that some chemicals move from end to end inside the cell and keep the ends from splitting. They are still working out how the split lands so close to the middle.

open_questions.q: Where did the old Egyptian signs for a half and a quarter of a grain measure come from?
open_questions.why_open: For about ninety years, books said they came from a picture of an eye. In 2002 a historian showed that this is unlikely. Nobody knows where they did come from.

maths.problem: 10 groundnuts are shared equally between two children. How many does each child get?
maths.explain: Share them one by one: one for the first child, one for the second, until none are left. Each child has 5. 5 and 5 make 10. So half of 10 is 5.
maths.context: In the Half Test you shared beans between two plates, one at a time. This is the same sharing, with groundnuts and two children.
maths.why_maths: Finding half of a group is the first kind of dividing. It tells you a fair share for two.

maths.problem: Two sisters each got 6 murukkus from a tin. That was half of the tin each. How many murukkus were in the tin?
maths.explain: The two halves are 6 and 6. Two halves make the whole. 6 and 6 make 12. So the tin had 12 murukkus.
maths.context: In Half Bingo you found half of numbers such as 12. This problem goes the other way: you know the half and find the whole.
maths.why_maths: Adding a number to itself is called doubling. Doubling undoes halving, so it lets you check any half.

maths.problem: A dosa is torn into a big piece and a small piece. Is the big piece half of the dosa? Say why.
maths.answer: No. The pieces are unequal, so neither one is a half.
maths.explain: A half is one of two equal parts. Lay the small piece on the big piece. The big piece sticks out. So these are two unequal parts, not two halves.
maths.context: In the Half Test you cut paper dosa A far from the middle and laid one piece on the other. This problem asks about the same kind of cut.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two parts tells you whether a share is fair before anyone starts eating.

maths.problem: 9 bananas are shared equally between two sisters. How many whole bananas does each get? What can they do with the one left over?
maths.answer: 4 whole bananas each, and 1 left over. They can cut it in half, so each gets 4 and a half.
maths.explain: Share them one by one. Each sister gets 4, and that uses 8 bananas. 1 is left over. A banana can be cut, so cut it into two halves. Each sister gets 4 bananas and half a banana.
maths.context: In the Half Test, 7 beans and 9 beans each left one bean over. This problem asks what to do when the thing left over can be cut.
maths.why_maths: Knowing which numbers leave one over tells you before you start whether you will need to cut something.

rows.label: left over, to cut in half

maths.problem: You fold a towel in half. Then you fold it in half again. When you open it, how many equal parts do the folds show? What is each part called?
maths.answer: 4 equal parts. Each part is a quarter.
maths.explain: The first fold makes 2 halves. The second fold halves each of those, so there are 2 and 2, which is 4 parts. One of four equal parts is called a quarter.
maths.context: In Fold the Washing you folded a towel in half and in half again. This problem asks you to count the parts without the towel.
maths.why_maths: Halving again and again is how people share one thing among 4 or 8 without measuring.
