roots.context: We cut paper dosas, shared beans and folded cloth to make halves. Now let us think about what a half really is.

deep_truth.truth: In the Half Test, you folded a paper dosa and cut it. Lay one piece on the other and look closely. They nearly match, but not perfectly. Nobody can cut a real thing into two perfectly equal parts. So people agree on 'equal enough', and call each part a half.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'half' is exact. With numbers it is: half of 8 is 4. With a real dosa, a half is something people agree on. It means the two parts are so close that nobody wants to swap.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Half Test, the paper dosa you cut by eye did not match, and even the folded one had edges that were a little off. In Share the Snack, the banana halves were not perfectly equal, but they were fair.

three.who_am_i: You have two hands, two eyes and two ears. Your left side and your right side look like two halves. Hold your palms together. They nearly match, but not perfectly. You are one whole child, not two halves.
three.what_is_life: You began as one tiny cell. That cell split into two cells, and those split into four. Every living thing you can see grew in this way, by cells splitting in two.
three.what_is_this_world: Right now, about half of the Earth is in sunlight and about half is in the dark. Day and night are two parts of one turning Earth.

roots.thread: Before you cut, there is one dosa. After you cut, there are two halves. Put them together and there is one dosa again. Nothing was added and nothing was lost. One thing can be seen as two parts, and two parts can be seen as one thing.

teachings.teaching: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says that in the beginning there was one Self alone, who became two. The sage Yajnavalkya said each of us is like one half of a split pea.
teachings.link: A split pea is a grain of dal. You saw that each grain of dal is one half of a seed, and that two halves fit together to make one whole seed.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says that to share your food and to care for the many living beings is the first of all the good things the wise have taught.
teachings.link: Halving is how sharing begins. The moment you make two equal parts of your dosa, there is enough for one more.

science.text: No measurement is perfectly exact. Every ruler and every scale has a smallest step it can show. So nobody can prove that two real things are exactly equal, only that they are equal as closely as the tool can tell.
Is an exact half real, or only an idea people share? Mathematicians and thinkers still argue about this.

other_view.who: Plato, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,400 years ago, and many mathematicians since
other_view.view: They say the exact half is real, even though no knife can cut it. Half of 8 is 4 for everyone, everywhere, and nobody voted on that. They say the two dosa pieces are rough copies of a perfect half. You can only tell that the pieces are 'not quite equal' because you already know what equal means.

practice.title: Two hands, one breath
practice.say: Sit still. Press your two palms together, finger to finger. Look closely. Is one hand a little bigger? Now close your eyes. Breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out slowly while I count to four. In and out are the two halves of one breath. Do it five times. Were the two halves the same each time?
practice.kid: Press your palms together. Do your hands match? Close your eyes. Breathe in for four counts. Breathe out for four counts. Do it five times.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people write down a half long ago? This card tells the true story of a grain measure in Egypt, and of a mistake that stayed in books for about ninety years.
how_we_found_out.story: More than 3,500 years ago, people in Egypt measured grain with a tub called a hekat. For smaller amounts they halved it, and halved it again. That gave a half, a quarter, an eighth, and so on down to one part in sixty-four. The people who kept the records wrote each of these six parts with its own sign. In 1911 a German scholar, Georg Möller, said the six signs were the six pieces of a well-known Egyptian picture, the Eye of Horus. It was a neat idea, and books repeated it for about ninety years. In 1923 another scholar, T. Eric Peet, pointed out a problem. The eye pieces do not turn up in writing until long after the grain signs. In 2002 Jim Ritter, a historian of mathematics, compared the handwritten signs from many hundreds of years. The older the writing was, the less the signs looked like pieces of an eye. So the signs very likely did not come from the eye. What is certain is the halving.
how_we_found_out.who: The record keepers of ancient Egypt, and later Georg Möller, T. Eric Peet and Jim Ritter
how_we_found_out.when: More than 3,500 years ago, and 1911 to 2002
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The Egyptian signs for a half, a quarter and the smaller parts of a grain measure were pieces of the Eye of Horus. Jim Ritter showed in 2002 that this is unlikely. The oldest handwritten signs look least like pieces of an eye.

PSICIC: noise and asymmetry in bacterial division revealed by computational image analysis at sub-pixel resolution. PLoS Computational Biology 4(11), e1000233. (Wild-type E. coli place the division site with a standard deviation of 2.9 percent of cell length.)
Min system of E. coli: Min proteins move from pole to pole and stop the division ring from forming at the ends of the cell (standard textbook account, checked on Wikipedia, 'Min System').
Human embryo: the first division falls about 24 to 36 hours after fertilisation, with four cells at about day two (Virtual Human Embryo, Stage 2, and NCBI Bookshelf NBK554562).
Seeds with two halves: groundnut, chickpea and pigeon pea are dicots, whose seeds have two cotyledons. Toor dal is split, skinned pigeon pea (general botany, not looked up for this unit).

Equinox: day and night are close to equal but not exactly equal, because the Sun is a disc and the air bends its light (timeanddate.com, 'Equinox: Almost Equal Day and Night', and the US Naval Observatory equinox page).

Eye of Horus and the hekat signs: Möller (1911), Peet (1923), and Ritter, J. (2002), 'Closing the Eye of Horus: the rise and fall of Horus-eye fractions', in Under One Sky, Ugarit-Verlag, pages 297 to 323. Read through the summary in Wikipedia, 'Eye of Horus', not the original paper.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a parent and a six-year-old in a flat. The Half Test uses three newspaper circles, scissors, 12 beans and two plates. A cut by eye comes out a little unequal nearly every time, and a folded cut matches closely, which is the result the test needs. If the eye cut happens to match, cut another. Half Bingo always ends: all ten cards cover all nine boxes, and a row usually comes after five to seven cards. Roll and Share was played in the head: an even roll gives 1 to 6 beans and an odd roll gives 1, so 12 beans takes about five or six turns each, and 50 beans in the bank is enough for two players. Use 70 beans for four players. The hanger balance in the dough challenge shows a difference of a pinch of dough only if the two cups hang the same distance from the hook, so level it empty first. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 2008 E. coli division study, the timing of the first cell divisions, the Eye of Horus story (from a Wikipedia summary of Ritter 2002, not the paper), the Tamil fraction words, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.3, Thirukkural 322, the equinox, sugarcane sweetness, the Pro Kabaddi halves and cutting on the fold. Not looked up: that about half of the Earth is lit at any moment, that the Moon looks half-lit about a week after new Moon, and that groundnut and dal seeds have two halves. These are standard facts. The three videos were confirmed by id, title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it.
